classic-story.name: Classic Story
classic-story.summary: Movie-style narrative arc applied to any topic: open the scene, introduce the villain, raise the stakes, send in the hero, deliver the plan, and close with hope. A versatile go-to when you need to make information feel like a story.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Capture attention with a vivid moment, image, or question that sets the world of the story. The audience should immediately know what kind of room they're in. Avoid agendas — the opening is the first scene, not a preamble.

beats.name: Context
beats.description: Establish what's normal in this world before anything goes wrong. Just enough background for the audience to feel the stakes when the villain shows up. Keep it tight; backstory is fuel, not the engine.

beats.name: Villain
beats.description: Introduce the antagonist — a problem, a competitor, a market force, an inertia. Give it a face and a name where you can. The clearer the villain, the more the audience cares about how the story turns out.

beats.name: Despair
beats.description: Show what's at risk if the villain wins. Emphasize the human or business cost of inaction. Don't rush past this beat — the discomfort here is what makes the resolution land.

beats.name: Hero
beats.description: Reveal the hero of the story. Often this is the audience themselves, your team, or your product. Frame the hero by what they uniquely bring to the fight, not by their résumé.

beats.name: Plan
beats.description: Walk through how the hero defeats the villain. Concrete, sequential, credible. Generic plans signal weak heroes; specific plans earn belief that the ending you're promising is reachable.

beats.name: Closing
beats.description: End with the resolution and the lesson. Show what the world looks like after the villain loses, and leave the audience with the feeling — and the line — they'll repeat afterwards.

executive.name: Executive
executive.summary: C-suite and senior leadership focused on strategic decisions, ROI, and big-picture outcomes. Highly time-constrained.
executive.description: C-suite and senior leaders deciding on strategy, ROI, and big-picture outcomes with very little time. Lead with the conclusion and keep to one insight per slide; set the key numbers in bold type and use as few bullet points as possible. Keep chart density low and the deck to 10-15 slides at most.

marketing.name: Marketing
marketing.summary: Marketing professionals analyzing campaign performance, brand metrics, and growth strategies.
marketing.description: Marketing professionals reviewing campaign performance, brand metrics, and growth strategy. Make the funnel visible, highlight engagement metrics, keep the brand consistent, and tell the story visually. Moderate chart density; 15-30 slides.

align.name: Align
align.summary: Create shared understanding and commitment across people who need to move together.
align.description: Use when stakeholders need a common view of goals, constraints, priorities, or responsibilities. Emphasize shared language, explicit tradeoffs, and next steps.
align.outcome: Stakeholders leave with the same priorities and operating assumptions.
successCriteria: Owners and next steps are clear

persuasive.name: Persuasive
persuasive.summary: Argument-led voice for sales, fundraising, and recommendation-driven decks.
persuasive.description: Frame every section as an argument that builds toward an ask. Surface objections, answer them, and pair claims with the strongest available proof. Read more like a memo than a report.
voiceCues: Lead each section with the claim it's making.
Surface the strongest counter-argument and address it.
Pair every claim with proof — customer, benchmark, or analyst.
End on a clear ask with named owner and date.
avoid: Symmetrical 'on one hand / on the other' framing without a verdict.
Information for its own sake — every chart should advance the argument.
Passive endings without a clear ask.
samplePhrases: Adopting our runtime cuts inference latency 8× while preserving accuracy.
The most common objection — 'we'll be locked in' — is addressed by our open OPF spec.
We're asking for a $30M Series B to ship into the enterprise tier.

classic.name: Classic
classic.description: A timeless, clean, and versatile theme with balanced color contrasts and classic typography. Ideal for professional, readable presentations.

steel-blue.name: Steel Blue
steel-blue.summary: Cool steel blues for credible, data-forward presentations.
steel-blue.description: A steel-blue palette that combines credibility, precision, and calm. Useful for analysis-heavy decks.

cool-horizon.name: Cool Horizon
cool-horizon.summary: Cool blue-green palette tuned for professional business decks.
cool-horizon.description: A balanced cool-toned scheme with deep navy, business blues, and teal accents. It works well across strategy, finance, and technical narratives.

tenorite.name: Tenorite
tenorite.description: Tenorite is a sans serif OPF font scheme for Latin presentations, using Tenorite Display for headings with Tenorite for body text.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

table-beside.name: Table beside
table-beside.summary: A table with commentary beside it.
table-beside.description: Place a table beside its interpretation. Use the supporting text to explain the conclusion without repeating every cell.

timeline.name: Timeline
timeline.summary: Dated events or a roadmap along one axis, with optional notes.
timeline.description: Show events or milestones in chronological order. Label each item with a date or stage and a concise description.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
